OWN-01.question: Which downdrag defaults should stand: UFC's procedure as the default basis, the materiality thresholds, and initial or final stress for skin friction?
OWN-01.why: The neutral-plane basis sets the drag load in the structural check. On test case DD-1 the bases range from 151 kN (plane at the bearing-layer top) to 409 kN (plane at the toe). Every basis is now shown; the default decides which number an answer leads with.
OWN-01.background: Commit a282d48 (master, unreleased) makes every cited basis an option: force equilibrium at 100/50/0 % toe mobilization (UFC 3-220-20 §6-7.4, §6-5.8.4.2; GEC-12 §7.3.6.1), settlement compatibility (UFC Fig 6-19), bearing-layer top, pile toe (upper bound) and Endo ratios (CGPR #56). Every run reports all of them; a judgment block appears when planes differ by more than max(0.5 m, 5 % of L) or drag by more than max(10 kN, 10 %). Default `auto` follows UFC: force equilibrium, or settlement compatibility when the curves do not cross. 5.33.0 already ships that compatibility fix (DD-1: 409 to 151 kN). UFC App. B-5.5 is reproduced (planes 47.8/50.2/52.5 ft vs 48/50/52). Skin friction uses initial effective stress by default; UFC §6-7.4 step 2 uses final.

options.label: Keep auto, thresholds and initial stress
options.effect: Numbers stay as validated (V-004, UFC App. B-5.5). The comparison and judgment block still show every basis with its citation.

options.label: Keep auto, switch to final stress
options.effect: Matches UFC §6-7.4 step 2 (Siegel et al. 2013). Beta friction and drag rise; V-004 and the smoke-test keys need re-checking before release.

options.label: No default: the engineer always picks
options.effect: Every run returns the comparison with a judgment block and the agent must state the basis it used. Nothing is chosen silently; answers get longer.

options.label: Change the materiality thresholds
options.effect: Give new values (now 0.5 m or 5 % of L for the plane; 10 kN or 10 % for drag). Tighter flags more cases for judgment.

OWN-01.recommendation: Keep `auto` and the thresholds: UFC governs DoD work and every alternative is already shown with its citation, so nothing is silent. Confirm settlement compatibility (it removed a 2.7x drag overstatement on DD-1). Adopt final stress only after re-running V-004 to see the shift.
OWN-01.if_no_answer: The next release ships `auto` (UFC's procedure), today's thresholds and initial stress, with the comparison and judgment block on every run.
sources: downdrag/DESIGN.md (Neutral-plane methods; Options, comparison and the default)

OWN-02.question: Should fem2d measure construction movements from the end of stage 0 by default, treating stage 0 as the gravity stage?
OWN-02.why: It decides whether reported settlements include the ground's own weight. On the test strip footing the footing stage alone settles 15.9 mm, but the cumulative movement is 49.3 mm because 33.4 mm is gravity. Quoting the wrong one triples the settlement.
OWN-02.background: Commit 4bf710c (master, unreleased) gives every stage three movements: its own (delta), cumulative from the start, and since a reference stage. `reset_displacements_after` sets the reference; if nobody sets it, the reference is the end of stage 0, assumed to be the initial gravity/K0 stage. Soil placed later (a fill group) is its own stage, so its self-weight movement shows there. When the default changes the final movement by more than 5 % and 0.1 mm, the result carries a judgment block with both numbers. The same commit fixed three bugs: resets never took effect, new fill inherited earlier movement as strain, and an unchanged plastic stage moved 1.5 %. 5.33.0 already made the consolidation settlement load-only.

options.label: Confirm: measure from end of stage 0
options.effect: Construction movements exclude the existing ground's self-weight unless a stage places soil. All three bases stay in the result, with a judgment block when the default matters.

options.label: Default to cumulative from the start
options.effect: Reported settlement includes the gravity movement of the existing ground (49.3 mm instead of 15.9 mm on the test case). Rarely what a designer wants.

options.label: Confirm, with a guard on stage 0
options.effect: As confirming, but if stage 0 carries loads or excavation, measure from the start and warn. A small extra build.

OWN-02.recommendation: Confirm the default with the guard (option 3). Excluding the initial gravity movement is common FE practice (the design note says so), all three bases are reported anyway, and the guard covers a model whose first stage is not a gravity stage.
OWN-02.if_no_answer: The next release measures from the end of stage 0 by default; results carry all three movement bases and a judgment block when the choice matters.

OWN-58.question: Should the downdrag load curve include the pile's own weight, as the module does now, or leave it out, as UFC 3-220-20 and GEC-12 do?
OWN-58.why: The pile's weight above the neutral plane adds to the drag force and the maximum load the module reports. UFC Fig 6-26, GEC-12 §7.3.6.1 and both worked examples draw the load curve as dead load plus negative skin friction only, so the module's numbers sit slightly above theirs.
OWN-58.background: On test case DD-1 the pile weight adds 24 kN. On V-004 (GEC-12 Vol III example) the module gives NP 53.6 ft, maximum load 490 kips, drag force 289 kips with the weight in, and 54.0 ft, 486.6 kips, 285.6 kips with it out, against the published 54 ft, 486 kips, 285 kips. Either way the setting stays available (pile_unit_weight = 0 leaves it out). Two related defaults to settle at the same time: the downdrag tool assumes concrete (24 kN/m3) while its default stiffness is steel's, and the calc package assumes steel (78.5 kN/m3).

options.label: Leave it out by default, as the references do
options.effect: Numbers match UFC, GEC-12 and the worked examples. The pile's weight can still be added with one setting.

options.label: Keep it in by default (today)
options.effect: Drag force and maximum load include the pile's weight above the neutral plane: slightly higher than the references (24 kN on DD-1, 4 kips on V-004).

OWN-58.recommendation: Leave it out by default, to match the cited references and their worked examples, and state in every result whether the pile's weight is included.
OWN-58.if_no_answer: The pile's weight stays in the load curve, and results sit slightly above the references' numbers.
sources: downdrag/DESIGN.md (comparison with CGPR #56, item 2; validation V-004)

OWN-03.question: Three copyrighted standards PDFs sit in the public references repo: keep them with a provenance note, remove the PDFs, or remove more?
OWN-03.why: AASHTO 1993 and the two Eurocode 7 parts are copyrighted. Anyone can download them from the public GitHub repo, and text extracted from them ships in the MIT-licensed package on PyPI. That is a licensing exposure for you, not a technical problem.
OWN-03.background: Tracked in geotech-references since commit 4c64e25 (2026-07-15): docs/aashto1993.pdf (30.6 MB), the EN 1997-2 PDF (5.6 MB) and the EN 1997-1 PDF (3.4 MB). Code comments call both Eurocode files public.resource.org copies; the AASHTO file's source is not recorded; there is no licence note. The wheel ships each module's chapter text (about 950 KB of JSON for the three) and lookup tables, not the PDFs. The app's pavement_design module and three agent adapters depend on these modules. Deleting a file does not remove it from git history; only a history rewrite and force-push would, and wheels already on PyPI keep their text. The other 36 tracked PDFs are government publications.

options.label: Keep, add a provenance note
options.effect: No code change. A note records the public.resource.org source; the AASHTO source stays unknown. The exposure is unchanged.

options.label: Remove the three PDFs only
options.effect: Files leave the repo from now on (still in history). Modules, text and lookups keep working; figure read-off takes the PDFs from SharePoint instead.

options.label: Remove PDFs and the chapter text
options.effect: Keeps the numeric lookups, drops copied prose from future wheels. Reference search loses these three standards; needs a refs release.

options.label: Also purge from git history
options.effect: Rewrites the refs repo history and force-pushes. Removes past copies on GitHub; forks and published wheels keep theirs. Disruptive; combine with option 2 or 3.

OWN-03.recommendation: Option 2 now, and consider option 3: move the PDFs to the SharePoint primary_references folder, where the app already fetches reference PDFs, and record their source. The numeric lookups are the most defensible part; copied chapter text in an MIT wheel is the hardest to defend.
OWN-03.if_no_answer: The PDFs stay public and the text keeps shipping with each refs release; nothing is deleted without your word.

OWN-04.question: Does DT accept PyMuPDF's AGPL-3.0 licence for an internal app hosted on Tiny Apps?
OWN-04.why: Every document tool (open, read, search, render, markups) runs on PyMuPDF. If DT's licence scan blocks AGPL after testers start, Document Review stops. Replacing it means rebuilding the whole document layer, so the answer is wanted before the tester deploy.
OWN-04.background: PyMuPDF is dual-licensed by Artifex: AGPL-3.0 for free, or a paid commercial licence. planlens is MIT, but that does not change PyMuPDF's terms; 26 planlens source files import it. It already installs through Nexus and runs on Funhouse. Corporate licence scanners flag AGPL, mainly for its network-use clause on web apps. The 2026-09-14 package survey's advice: ask DT once before Tiny Apps; do not switch pre-emptively. The permissive fallback is pypdfium2 (Apache/BSD) with pypdf and pdfplumber, at the cost of the entire document layer. Related trap: pymupdf4llm and pymupdf-layout are non-commercial licences; they are not used and must not be installed.
OWN-04.recommendation: Ask now, in writing, with the facts in the message. Do not switch libraries unless DT says no; if they do, ask whether an Artifex commercial licence is acceptable before anyone plans a rewrite.
OWN-04.if_no_answer: Testers start on PyMuPDF anyway; a later DT block would take Document Review offline until a licence or a rewrite.
OWN-04.message_to_send: Hi - before our Tiny Apps pilot (Document Review) opens to more testers: the app's PDF layer uses PyMuPDF (Python package 'pymupdf', by Artifex), licensed AGPL-3.0 or commercially. It is installed from Nexus, unmodified, and used internally only. Is AGPL-3.0 acceptable for this use, or would you need a commercial licence or a different library? We would rather know now than after testers depend on it. Thanks.
sources: module_work/PLANLENS_PACKAGE_SURVEY.md (Plain-English summary; Part C, licensing facts)

OWN-07.question: Confirm or correct the seven DRAFT house rules the narrative reader follows when answering your standing report questions.
OWN-07.why: The rules decide how the reader answers where a report is silent or ambiguous, and its scores are measured against your own answer keys. Where a rule differs from how you wrote the keys, a correct reading is scored as a failure.
OWN-07.background: report_ingest/narrative_glossary.py holds seven rules, all DRAFT and all in force: (1) explorations the report says were not done count 0, not null; (2) null means the report does not say, never 'none' or 'N/A'; (3) the three 'mention' fields mean the work was done for the project (site response means a site-specific analysis, not a code site class); (4) soilCorrosion is the finding (yes, no or mixed, plus the basis); (5) postName is the city only, null for outside projects; (6) primeAe is the architect-engineer of record, not the geotechnical firm or contractor; (7) earthHazardsExposed uses the listed phrases and never seismic shaking. After rules 3-4 were re-read from your keys (2026-10-04), the next run went from 75/77 % to 83/85 % recall/precision.

options.label: Confirm all seven
options.effect: Status becomes CONFIRMED; answers do not change. The prompt stops marking the rules as unconfirmed.

options.label: Correct some rules
options.effect: Name the rule and the right reading. It changes the answers and the scores on the next Foundry run, and nothing else.

OWN-07.recommendation: Check rules 1, 3 and 7 first: they touch the most fields, including the exploration counts. The others follow your keys as already read.
OWN-07.if_no_answer: All seven stay in force marked DRAFT; nothing breaks, but the scores keep resting on the lead's reading of your keys.

OWN-08.question: What counts as a structure for structureCount, and does figureCount include figures in appendices?
OWN-08.why: Both are scored against your answer keys. The reader got structureCount right on only 3 of 8 reports and tends to over-count; figureCount was wrong on 4 of 8 in an earlier run. Without your definition nobody can tell whether the reader or the rule is wrong.
OWN-08.background: Both fields come from your standing query schema. The narrative reader answers structureCount from the report text; the only rule is the DRAFT 'count 0 when the report says none'. figureCount is counted in code from figure captions and given to the reader as a fact; the reader answers from the report's own list of figures and any disagreement is recorded. Run 7 (September): figureCount, structureCount and structureList each wrong on 4 of 8. Foundry run 2 (2026-10-07): structureCount 3/8, structureList 3/7 with one invented. RI-08 notes figureCount could come from the page labels instead.

options.label: Items in structureList
options.effect: The two fields always agree; the definition of a structure lives in structureList (each structure the report gives recommendations for).

options.label: Another definition (state it in the notes)
options.effect: For example only new buildings, or every named facility; written as a CONFIRMED rule and applied on the next run.

options.label: Includes appendix figures
options.effect: Counts every captioned figure, main body and appendices alike.

options.label: Main-body figures only
options.effect: Counts the figures in the report's own list of figures; appendix plates and logs are left out.

OWN-08.recommendation: Tell us the rule you used when writing the answer keys; matching it is the point. If you had none, option 1 keeps the two structure fields consistent.
OWN-08.if_no_answer: The reader keeps guessing; structureCount stays near 3 of 8, and its misses can be neither fixed nor blamed on the reader.

OWN-09.question: Which page-labelling policy and label-review mode should report ingest use by default, or should it wait for more blind labels?
OWN-09.why: Page labels decide which reader sees each page; a wrong label means a log or lab sheet is never read. The current defaults are not supported by the measurements, and the paid label review lost accuracy on the latest run.

options.label: Keep structural plus disagreement review

options.label: Rules only, no review
options.effect: Best in-sample score and no vision or review spend; slightly worse on the 60 blind pages.

options.label: Decide after more blind pages
options.effect: Use the R39 PDF (153 pages already hand-labelled, never used) as a blind set first (OWN-39), then pick.

OWN-09.recommendation: Option 3, with no rush while ingest is parked: R39's 153 labelled pages are the cheapest way to settle it. Meanwhile consider switching the disagreement review off, since it lost accuracy on the latest run.
OWN-09.if_no_answer: Defaults stay structural with the disagreement review; nothing runs while report ingest is parked.

OWN-17.question: What should the rapid-drawdown stage-3 default be: keep 'fellenius', switch to 'gle', or report both?
OWN-17.why: It sets the factor of safety on rapid-drawdown checks. On the published test case the default gives 1.273 against 1.443 (12 % low, conservative); the opt-in 'gle' gives 1.370 (5 % low). You kept 'fellenius' on 2026-07-08 while checking your notes.
OWN-17.background: Three-stage rapid drawdown (Duncan, Wright and Brandon). Stage 3 needs an effective normal stress on each slice. The default 'fellenius' uses the Fellenius/OMS slice estimate; 'gle' uses the rigorous GLE normal from stage 1, and falls back to 'fellenius' if the drained GLE does not converge. The specialist who diagnosed it (2026-07-07) called the Fellenius estimate an outright bug because it is inconsistent with stage 1. You recalled a substantive reason for the cruder estimate and planned to check your graduate-school notes. Published case: #96 (V-038), 1.443.

options.label: Keep 'fellenius' (notes support it)
options.effect: Default unchanged and conservative; 'gle' stays opt-in. Record the reason from your notes.

options.label: Switch the default to 'gle'
options.effect: Closer to published values (1.370 vs 1.443); drawdown factors of safety rise; validation pins updated.

options.label: Report both, default unchanged
options.effect: Every run returns both stage-3 results with a judgment note, as downdrag now does; nothing silent.

OWN-17.recommendation: Option 3: it follows your rule that methods with several accepted bases are shown side by side, keeps the conservative default, and lets your notes settle the default later.
OWN-17.if_no_answer: 'fellenius' stays the default (conservative); 'gle' stays opt-in and unmentioned in results.

OWN-18.question: Make the PyNiteFEA frame-analysis package an optional extra, so cluster installs stop upgrading numpy and numba?
OWN-18.why: PyNiteFEA alone forces numpy from the cluster's 2.1.3 to 2.4.6, which drags numba and llvmlite up and leaves four notebook packages unsatisfied in every install log. Harmless so far, but noisy, and it may matter on hosts with a fixed numpy.
OWN-18.background: Settled in the install guide: PyNiteFEA 3.1.0 requires numpy 2.4.0 or later; numba caps numpy below 2.5, so the resolver lands on 2.4.6; numba goes 0.61 to 0.67 and llvmlite 0.44 to 0.49 (numba 0.67 verified numerically identical for pystrata). Nothing else needs numpy above 2.1.3, so moving this one dependency removes four of the install log's conflict warnings. Cost: frame analysis (continuous beams, 2D/3D frames) would need an extra at install; the module already hides itself when PyNite is missing. Since 5.8.1 a plain install brings the whole stack, at your request. EV-08 (a Foundry eval where numpy 1.26 broke 17 questions) might benefit; not verified.

options.label: Yes, make it an optional extra
options.effect: Cluster installs keep numpy 2.1.3; frame analysis needs the extra. Breaks 'a plain install brings everything' for this one package.

options.label: No, keep it in core
options.effect: Install logs keep the four known, harmless warnings.

OWN-18.recommendation: Yes, unless you use frame analysis on the cluster. The cascade causes four of the install log's warnings, and the module already degrades cleanly without PyNite.
OWN-18.if_no_answer: PyNiteFEA stays in core; every cluster install keeps upgrading numpy and numba.

OWN-19.question: Should lateral_pile get a cracked or moment-curvature pile stiffness, or should the V-017 residual be closed as accepted?
OWN-19.why: Reinforced-concrete piles and shafts crack under lateral load; uncracked stiffness underestimates deflection, which is unconservative. The validation case already passes, so this is about the general capability, not that test.
OWN-19.background: V-017 (grout-filled casing pile vs an LPILE run): with the composite uncracked stiffness (EI 8,109 kN·m², 1.13 times the casing alone) the head deflection is 3.60 mm vs published 3.3 mm, +9.2 %, a pass within the ±10 % band. The validation note blames the residual on LPILE's nonlinear (cracked) EI. That looks backwards: a softer cracked EI would raise our 3.60 mm further above 3.3 mm, so the residual's real cause is unknown. lateral_pile today offers composite_section_ei (uncracked, an upper-bound stiffness) and no moment-curvature analysis. Pending since v5.3 (July).

options.label: Build moment-curvature EI
options.effect: LPILE-style nonlinear EI for RC piles and shafts; realistic deflections at high moment. Medium build plus validation cases.

options.label: Add a simple cracked-EI option
options.effect: For example ACI 318's reduced moments of inertia; small build, cited basis, shown beside the uncracked result.

options.label: Close V-017 as accepted
options.effect: No build; results keep uncracked stiffness, documented as an upper bound.

OWN-19.recommendation: Option 2 now, reported beside the uncracked value with its citation; option 1 later if RC drilled-shaft work is common. Close V-017 as a pass and correct the note about the residual's cause.
OWN-19.if_no_answer: lateral_pile keeps uncracked stiffness only; RC pile deflections at high load stay underestimated.

OWN-20.question: Add opt-in switches so three modules can match published examples, or keep the current defensible defaults?
OWN-20.why: Three validation cases differ from published examples by convention, not error. Anyone comparing the app with those references will see the gaps, up to 2x on drilled-shaft base resistance, and may distrust the module unless the basis is stated or selectable.
OWN-20.background: (1) V-008b drilled shaft: the module applies GEC-10's large-diameter base reduction (1.27/Db, a factor of 0.521 in the example); the example does not, so base resistance can differ up to 2x. The module is conservative. (2) V-021 bearing capacity: compute() is 17.6 % above the GEC-6 example because it applies Vesic depth factors (dq 1.10-1.20; the example uses 1.0) and its water-table model gives no reduction; the example's closed form is matched to 4 figures when assembled its way. The module is less conservative here. (3) V-002 driven pile: Tomlinson alpha about 0.42 in stiff clay (su about 1.9 ksf) vs 0.76 in the example; shaft 18-22 % low, conservative.

options.label: Opt-in switches, defaults unchanged
options.effect: Each choice becomes a named option with its citation; results state the basis used. Validation numbers unchanged.

options.label: Report both values side by side
options.effect: Results show the default and the reference-matching value together, as downdrag now does.

options.label: Leave as is
options.effect: The basis stays documented only in the validation notes.

OWN-20.recommendation: Report both values for the bearing-capacity depth factor, where the default is the less conservative one; opt-in switches for the other two. Either way the result should name its basis, per your rule against silent choices.
OWN-20.if_no_answer: Defaults stay; the gaps stay explained only in validation_examples/RESULTS.md.

OWN-21.recommendation: Option 2: soldier-pile walls are routine excavation support and V-012 gives a ready validation case. Mark the other seven parked in one place, and do not replace the frost and dewatering references unless a project needs them.

OWN-22.question: Test the experimental model-setup agent (geo_project) yourself, park it formally, or retire it?
OWN-22.why: It has been built and switched off since June, unreachable from either page, while the slope and FEM modules moved on. It still costs tests and upkeep, and its gaps grow with each module change.
OWN-22.background: geo_project is a versioned project file for slope and FEM model setup: provenance tracking, a quarantine on vision-drafted geometry, 25+ validators, builders into the limit-equilibrium and FEM modules, DXF/PDF ingest and an echo-back drawing. A staged setup sub-agent asks for confirmation at each gate. It is off by default (enable_setup_agent=False) and the web app never turns it on. In June you kept it out of the presentation: 'haven't properly tested it'. Drift since (GM-37): no anisotropic su, pore-pressure points, stabilizing piles or tension cracks, and only the first surcharge reaches the slope model.

options.label: Test it in a session

OWN-22.recommendation: Park it formally. Document Review and Tiny Apps come first, and the project file is the groundwork for the parked modelling GUI, so deleting it would throw away that prerequisite.

OWN-23.why: The July industry memo said Streamlit is right 'until multi-user' and to discuss a FastAPI/React or Chainlit rebuild only then. Several testers on Tiny Apps meet that condition, so the item needs a ruling.
OWN-23.background: Memo recommendation 6 (July): a multi-user UI is 'N/A now; discuss only if that need appears'. options.effect: Decide once real concurrent use shows whether Streamlit holds up.

options.label: Plan a FastAPI/React rebuild
options.effect: A large effort, and a departure from CfA's Streamlit template.

OWN-26.question: The public app repo's field-feedback folder names include place names: make the repo private, or scrub the names?
OWN-26.why: Three of the seven tracked field-feedback folders are named after a project's location, and those names also appear in at least 22 tracked files and at least 12 commit messages. Anyone browsing the public GitHub repo can see where the office works.

OWN-28.question: Merge or drop the June rescue branch of reference chapter text and summaries in geotech-references, after a lead reviews it?
OWN-28.why: Six GECs have no section summaries (0 of 670 sections), so search shows bare titles. The branch covers four of them and adds missing chapters, about 3,300 lines never reviewed. It is the quickest gain in what the references sub-agent can find.
OWN-28.background: Branch rescue/reference-wip-2026-06-02 (one commit, 7fb6fe8, on origin) was cut from refs 1.2.5 in June; main is now 1.4.1. It changes 51 files (+3,287 lines): GEC-7 chapters 6-10 and GEC-12 Vol II chapters 9-18, summaries for GEC-6/7/12/13, and a script add_gec13_summaries.py. Main has GEC-7 chapters 1-5 and GEC-12 chapters 1-8. Since June, main has changed only one of the branch's files (CLAUDE.md), so a merge should be nearly conflict-free. The text was agent-built and never checked against the PDFs; the weekend QC routine appears never to have run (OWN-33). The source GECs are FHWA publications.

options.label: Lead reviews, then merge
options.effect: A lead spot-checks sections against the PDFs, fixes errors and merges for the next refs release. Better section search and chapter retrieval.

options.label: Merge as is
options.effect: Fastest; unreviewed text reaches the references sub-agent and the PyPI package.

options.label: Drop the branch
options.effect: Nothing gained; the text would be rebuilt from scratch if ever wanted.

OWN-28.recommendation: Option 1. The content is FHWA text with no merge conflicts; a sampled check against the PDFs is cheap, and summaries are what make section search useful.

OWN-59.question: In a slope analysis, when an anchor, nail or geosynthetic would pull the sliding mass toward failure rather than hold it back, should it count as a driving force, or as slack (no force)?
OWN-59.why: Since 2026-10-14 every method counts a support's moment with its sign, as the GLE already did, so such a support is counted as driving. A tension element cannot push; in reality it would go slack and carry nothing. Counting it as driving gives a lower (more conservative) factor of safety than the element can cause.
OWN-59.background: It arises only where a support crosses the slip surface at an angle that makes its pull assist sliding, for example a steep nail near the crest of a deep circle. Piles (which can push) are not part of this question. The references read so far (Wright & Duncan 1991; the Slide2 help) do not say how a destabilising pull is treated.

options.label: Slack: no force
options.effect: A tension element whose pull would assist sliding is left out for that surface, and the result says which ones were. Matches what the element can carry.

options.label: Count as driving (now)
options.effect: Keeps the current, more conservative result; a support can lower the factor of safety below the unreinforced value on some surfaces.

options.label: Offer both
options.effect: An option on the analysis with a cited default; the result names which was used.

OWN-59.recommendation: Slack, for tension elements (nails, anchors, geosynthetics), with the result naming each support left out; piles unchanged.
OWN-59.if_no_answer: Supports keep counting with their sign (conservative).

OWN-61.question: How should the app's figures improve beyond today's plotting fixes: grow the one plotting tool, add a figure helper that drafts, looks and revises, or let the agent write plotting code in a locked box?
OWN-61.why: In the 2026-10-15 session the app's plans were not drawn to scale, footprints and boring names could not be shown, and you asked why Claude Code draws so much better. Claude Code writes its own plotting code and looks at the result; the app's agent can only call one plotting tool, and until today it drew lines and dots only.
OWN-61.background: Done today (master, unreleased; GM-90, TA-29): plans and sections at 1:1 scale, filled outlines, point names placed clear of each other, hover text, marker shapes, named cases as dots, legend off the map, and the chat card drawing charts in their own colours (the dark theme was hiding titles and axis labels). Before-and-after page: https://claude.ai/artifact/TcPujcvMF19HZQXtPVAmMj. On Tufte: the book itself cannot go into the model (copyright); a one-page checklist in our own words naming his principles (data-ink, chartjunk, small multiples, labels on the data) beside engineering conventions can.

options.label: A: keep growing the plotting tool
options.effect: Add the figures you make most (exceedance curves, profiles, tornado charts, probability maps) as tool options. Safe and cheap; limited to what is built in.

options.label: B: a figure helper (recommended next)
options.effect: A small helper with its own figure checklist draws, looks at the PNG and redraws, two or three times at most, behind an OFF switch until the suite shows it helps. About 3 to 6 extra model calls a figure.

options.label: C: plotting code in a locked box
options.effect: The agent writes matplotlib or Plotly code that runs with no network, no files outside the conversation and a time limit. Closest to Claude Code; it is code execution on a shared host, so the Tiny Apps team must agree first.

OWN-61.recommendation: A now (done), then B behind an OFF switch; C only if A and B fall short and the Tiny Apps team allows it.

OWN-62.question: Below a pile's toe, how deep should downdrag count the settlement caused by the pile's own load: UFC 3-220-20's rule or GEC-12's?
OWN-62.why: The module used to count a fixed 3 pile widths below the toe, which neither reference says. It now follows the references, and they give different depths.
OWN-62.background: UFC 3-220-20 (2025) §6-5.8.4.3, p. 449: the depth "is typically selected where the change in stress is less than 10% of the bearing stress of the equivalent footing" (for a single pile, about 2.2 pile widths below the toe). GEC-12 Vol I §7.3.5.3 step 1c, p. 324: "less than 10% of existing vertical effective stress at that depth" (deeper; in a sand example 5.4 m against UFC's 0.9 m, toe settlement 17.4 mm against 12.7 mm). Neither rule cuts off the fill: settlement from a fill or drawdown below the toe is counted to the bottom of the soil profile either way. Every result shows what both rules give.

options.label: UFC: 10 % of the bearing stress (current default)
options.effect: Matches the rest of the downdrag module, which follows UFC's procedure as the headline. Shallower toe zone.

options.label: GEC-12: 10 % of the effective stress
options.effect: Deeper toe zone, more toe settlement; the more conservative choice for a single pile.

options.label: Keep both, but warn when they differ by more than a set amount
options.effect: UFC stays the default; the result flags cases where the choice matters.

OWN-62.recommendation: Keep UFC as the default, as the module's headline method, with GEC-12's depth shown beside it in every result.
OWN-62.if_no_answer: UFC stays the default; both depths stay in every result.

OWN-63.question: Driven piles: five places where GEC-12 leaves a reading open. Which default should each take?

(1) Above the chart's su range p. 247 recommends API RP 2A for highly overconsolidated clays; GEC-12's own worked example (Vol 3 Table D-100) held Ca at the chart's end. With API, a published clay example's shaft comes out 25-53 % above it; at the chart's end, 1-13 %. (2) The printed D = 40b curve gives Ca slightly above su (alpha up to 1.1); API caps alpha at 1.0 (p. 252). (3) Step 8 (p. 243) limits the toe's effective stress to 3 ksf; a published example that did not apply it is 16 % higher at the toe. (4) p. 247 puts H-piles on the corrugated curve; the worked example used smooth steel. (5) Fig. 7-17's legend measures D from the ground surface; Step 1 speaks of the embedded length in clay.

options.label: Hold Ca at the chart's end (current default)
options.effect: Matches GEC-12's worked example; lower, conservative.

options.label: API RP 2A alpha
options.effect: p. 247's recommendation for highly overconsolidated clays; Ca jumps at the chart's end.

options.label: API only where the clay is highly overconsolidated (su / sigma'v > 1)
options.effect: Follows p. 247's condition literally; needs sigma'v, which the module has.

parts.label: 2. Ca above su inside the chart

options.label: Cap Ca at su (current default)
options.effect: alpha <= 1.0 as API; a published soft-over-stiff clay example within 1 %.

options.label: Read the printed curve as drawn
options.effect: alpha up to 1.1; that example 13 % above published.

parts.label: 3. Step 8's 3 ksf limit on the toe's effective stress

options.label: On by default (current)
options.effect: As GEC-12 prints it; deep sand toes lower.

options.label: Off by default, an option
options.effect: Matches older published examples; higher toe capacity.

options.label: Corrugated steel curve (current default)
options.effect: p. 247's text.

options.label: Smooth steel curve
options.effect: GEC-12's worked example's choice; lower adhesion.

options.label: From the ground surface (current default)
options.effect: The figure's legend.

options.label: From the top of the clay
options.effect: Step 1's 'embedded pile length in clay'; a smaller D/b, so the D = 10b curve sooner.

OWN-63.recommendation: Keep the current defaults: each is either GEC-12's printed text or its own worked example's basis, and on (1) and (2) the conservative side. The module states every one in its results, so the engineer sees the reading used.
OWN-63.if_no_answer: The current defaults stay, stated in every result's choices.

OWN-64.question: Cantilever wall: should a PERMANENT surcharge over the heel (an approach slab, pavement) count as holding the wall against sliding and overturning?
OWN-64.why: GM-157 made the wall leave a live-load surcharge over the heel out of the resisting forces, as every reference does. For a permanent surcharge the references differ, and the choice moves sliding and overturning factors of safety by about 10 % on a typical wall.
OWN-64.background: NHI-06-089 Vol II p. 10-41 (cantilever walls): "the surcharge loads are generally assumed to be located behind the heel of the wall, and conservatively neglected within the width of the base slab since they contribute to overturning and sliding resistance." p. 10-31 lists dead-load surcharges such as an approach slab or pavement. GEC-11 p. 4-22 (MSE walls, LRFD): "External loads that increase sliding resistance should only be included if those loads are permanent", taken at the minimum load factor (p. 4-4, ES minimum 0.75). Either way the surcharge's thrust still drives and it still loads the base for bearing; every result states the reading in its choices.

options.label: Leave it out of sliding and overturning (current default)
options.effect: NHI-06-089 p. 10-41, the cantilever-wall text; conservative.

options.label: Count it at full weight
options.effect: A permanent load resists; higher factors of safety.

options.label: Count it at its minimum load factor (0.75)
options.effect: The AASHTO / GEC-11 reading; between the two.

OWN-64.recommendation: Keep the current default: it is the cantilever-wall text's own reading and the conservative one, and `dead_load_resists=true` is there when a permanent slab is certain.
OWN-64.if_no_answer: The default stays, stated in every result's choices.

OWN-65.question: How should we judge whether the judgment-calls switch costs too much?
OWN-65.why: What the switch is: an option, off today, that changes how the agent handles the judgment calls in an engineering answer: which neutral-plane method to use, what strength to assume for a layer nobody tested, what factor of safety to aim for. With it on, the agent (1) lists each judgment call its answer turns on, (2) asks the references helper what the manuals say about each, and (3) states each call with its citation; a calc package then keeps the inputs you gave apart from the ones it assumed. With it off, the agent still makes those calls, from its own reading and usually without a citation. Why it is a decision now: the last live rerun showed the switch works (references looked up, citations reach the calc PDFs, given and assumed inputs printed right), but it fails the cost test it was set: run the same question with the switch off and on, and the on turn may cost at most 1.8 times the off turn. The switch's extra cost is roughly fixed, because the references lookup costs about $0.20-0.53 a turn whatever the question. A short chat question costs $0.11 with the switch off; 1.8 times allows $0.20, only $0.09 more, but the lookup alone adds at least $0.20, so the on turn costs 2.8 to 5.8 times as much and fails however well the switch behaves. On a calc package that already costs a few dollars, the same $0.20-0.53 is a small share and passes. So the test measures how cheap the question was, not whether the switch is worth its cost.
OWN-65.background: The measurements: rerun w14 (2026-10-19, $1.79) cost 2.87 times OFF on the two flows run, about 2.0-2.4 times over four flows. A short FEM question costs $0.11 with the switch off, and the lookup alone adds $0.20-0.53. The switch stays off until this is settled.

options.label: Keep the ratio (ON at most 1.8 times OFF)
options.effect: The switch stays off unless the lookup gets much cheaper.

options.label: An added cost per turn (for example at most $0.50 more for a turn that produces a deliverable)
options.effect: Judges what the lookup actually costs; short questions are not penalised for being cheap.

options.label: Look references up only for deliverables (calc packages, reports), not chat answers
options.effect: Chat answers cost what they do today; deliverables carry cited judgment calls.

OWN-65.recommendation: The added cost per turn, together with looking references up only for deliverables: a calc package is where a cited basis matters, and the cost is then bounded per deliverable.
OWN-65.if_no_answer: The switch stays OFF; the rest of the work behind it (given vs assumed inputs, unrunnable tools hidden) is already on.

OWN-66.question: Which printed passive earth pressure coefficients (log spiral) should the tools use by default?
OWN-66.why: The tools now offer two printed sources for log-spiral passive pressure. They agree at low friction angles but differ by 10-13 % above 40 degrees, and the default decides how much passive resistance a wall or sheet pile gets unless the user picks.
OWN-66.background: Caquot-Kerisel 1948 as the Caltrans Trenching and Shoring Manual prints it (Fig 4-20) is today's default. UFC 3-220-20 (current DoD criteria, the DM 7.2 successor) prints Fig 4-13 and Eq 4-12. The 1948 chart gives 1-4 % more passive up to 35 degrees and 10-13 % more at 40-45 (13.14 against 12.0 at 40 degrees). UFC footnote 21 says the 1948 reduction-factor approach used averages that introduced substantial inaccuracy. A sheet pile sized with UFC values would be embedded a little deeper.

options.label: Keep Caquot-Kerisel 1948 (Caltrans)
options.effect: No result changes; more passive resistance above 35 degrees.

options.label: UFC 3-220-20 (Fig 4-13 at wall friction 0.66 phi, Eq 4-12 otherwise)
options.effect: Lower passive above 35 degrees, deeper embedment; 1948 stays as an option.

OWN-66.recommendation: UFC 3-220-20: it is the current criteria and gives the lower (safer) passive resistance at high friction angles; keep 1948 as a named option.
OWN-66.if_no_answer: The default stays Caquot-Kerisel 1948; both are offered and the result names the source used.
sources: Caltrans T&S Fig 4-20 p. 4-30; UFC 3-220-20 Fig 4-13 p. 193, Eq 4-12 and fn 21 p. 191

OWN-67.question: At-rest earth pressure behind a slope: which printed formula should the tools use by default?
OWN-67.why: The two references the tools can use for at-rest pressure behind sloping ground give opposite answers: one lowers it, the other raises it. Today the tool asks the user to pick.
OWN-67.background: Caltrans Eq 4-3-14 prints K0 = (1 - sin phi)(1 - sin beta). EN 1997-1 Eq 9.2 prints K0 (1 + sin beta) for ground rising from the wall. Caltrans's own Fig 4-7 draws beta positive for rising ground, so this is not a sign convention. At phi 30 the Caltrans form falls below Caltrans's own active Rankine value above about a 16 degree slope, and UFC Table 4-3 also raises K0 behind a 2H:1V slope, so the Caltrans form is most likely a printing error.

options.label: EN 1997-1 Eq 9.2 by default; Caltrans as an option with a warning
options.effect: At-rest pressure behind rising ground goes up, as UFC also shows.

options.label: Keep asking the user each time
options.effect: No default; the call is refused until a form is named.

OWN-67.recommendation: EN 1997-1 Eq 9.2 by default, with the Caltrans form kept as an option that carries the warning.
OWN-67.if_no_answer: The tool keeps asking which form to use.

OWN-68.question: For lateral pile curves, from what undrained shear strength should a clay count as 'stiff'?
OWN-68.why: The soil-profile shortcut picks the soft-clay curve (Matlock) below 100 kPa and a stiff-clay curve from 100 kPa. That 100 kPa is the module's own number, and the FHWA manual it follows calls clays from about 48 kPa stiff, so a 48-96 kPa clay gets the soft-clay curve today.
OWN-68.background: FHWA GEC 9 (lateral loads) calls 250-500 psf (12-24 kPa) clays soft (p. 216) and 1,000-2,000 psf (48-96 kPa) clays stiff (p. 219); COM624P prints no boundary, and its stiff-clay tables start at 47.9 kPa. The boundary is now a caller setting (`stiff_clay_cu`), and the result states which curve each layer got and why. Only users of the soil-profile shortcut see the default; a direct call names its curve.

options.label: Keep 100 kPa
options.effect: No result changes; 48-100 kPa clays keep the soft-clay curve.

options.label: 48 kPa, GEC 9's lower bound for stiff clay
options.effect: 48-100 kPa clays get the stiff-clay curve (usually less deflection).

options.label: No default; ask each time
options.effect: The shortcut refuses until a boundary is named.

OWN-68.recommendation: 48 kPa, as GEC 9 prints it, with the setting kept so an engineer can change it.
OWN-68.if_no_answer: The default stays 100 kPa, stated in each result as the module's own number.
